findings.problem: In a forced palette the project's h1 - the one owner-written string at the head of the left column and the page's only h1 - loses the bottom 55-61% of its letterforms. Measured by painted pixels (not computed style) at deviceScaleFactor 2: the glyph band is 17 device rows at rest and 7 in forced colours, and the cut is a hard horizontal line. Reproduced on owner-flight, owner-editing, owner-undone, owner-draft, desk and print, in BOTH rooms, at 768/1152/1279/1280/1440 - ink coverage 1071-1260px drops to 419-479px (33-45%). It is clean at 390. Cause, isolated by bisect: hiding .b-num restores the name in full, and giving .b-who a stacking context restores it with zero geometry change. Chromium paints an opaque Canvas backplate behind text in forced-colors mode, sized to the font box, not the CSS line box. .b-num sets font-size 148px against line-height 133.2px (--lead-display 0.9), so its backplate overhangs its own box by ~5px and paints over the name sitting 20px above it. At 390 the count is 96px/86.4px and the overhang vanishes, which is exactly why nothing caught it. Nothing else on any of the fourteen states loses ink in a forced palette - a full element-by-element painted-ink sweep of both rooms returned this and only this. The keepsake (print) and the received desk view are both affected, so a guest in Windows High Contrast is handed a plan whose couple's name is sliced in half.
findings.fix: Add, at the end of b.css inside the existing @media (forced-colors: active) block: `.b-who { position: relative; z-index: 1; }`. That lifts the heading into the positioned-paint phase so the display number's backplate can no longer paint over it. Verified at 768 and 1440, paper and ink, on owner-flight, desk and print: the h1's painted ink returns to 1085-1086px (full) and .b-num's box stays at exactly the same y (267.69 at 1440, 145.19 on desk/print) - no pixel moves in either room in normal paint. Do not fix this by adding margin: 5px of extra clearance also works but changes the horizon composition at every width from 768 up.

findings.element: .b-skel slabs and the loading frame's column, state=loading at >=768
findings.problem: The loading frame is exact at 390 and wrong at every width above it. Measured, both rooms, loading vs the state that follows it: at 390 .b-who lands at (20,28) in both frames, the name-to-'Today is 16 July' offset is 252px in both, and the count slab is 107x86 against a real count block 86 tall - a perfect stand-in. At 768/1152/1280/1440 the loading frame is a 348px column centred in the room while the arrived surface is a 1066px document flush to the left margin, so every string the frame drew hops 113/305/359/359px LEFT and 12px DOWN the instant the data lands, and the name-to-today offset changes 252 -> 285 (delta 33px). The count slab stays frozen at the phone's 107x86 at every one of those widths while the real count arrives 133px tall - the skeleton under-draws the largest object on the page by 47px of height and then the page grows into it. The gate's own assertion 'nothing hops when the data lands' opens ONE page pair, loading vs phone at 390x844, and compares one relative offset; it is green on the only width where there is nothing to catch. This is the paid-for class 'Loading that promises the truth - skeletons sized to their real geometry' passing on an assertion that proves nothing.
findings.fix: Lay the loading frame out in the arrived surface's own column at every width instead of centring one phone-width card: render the skeleton inside the same .b-field / .b-two left column, top-aligned on the document's left margin (x=97 at 768/1152, 107 at 1280, 187 at 1440), and drive the count slab's height from --size-count at the current width rather than a literal 86 - 133px at >=768, 86px at 390. Keep .b-todayLabel at the same 285px offset below .b-who that the arrived surface uses at those widths (252px at 390). Then widen the gate assertion at interaction-check.mjs:1888-1915 to run the loading/arrived pair at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 and to compare .b-who's absolute x as well as the today offset, or it will go green on the fix and stay green on the next regression.

biggestWin: The keyboard model is finished, and it is finished in both rooms. Driven end to end at 1440 in paper and ink: Enter on a row's badge opens the editor and moves focus into the named panel; Escape closes it and puts focus back on the exact badge that opened it; the editor's tab order runs in visual order and every stop is scrolled into view; three stepper presses keep focus on the stepper and write 'Send the invitations moved 7 days earlier. Undo Ctrl Z' into a live region that names its own key; Ctrl+Z from a control undoes and disables the way back when the stack empties; delete hands focus to the next row rather than the body, and undo restores the moment in view with the row focused; the segment toggles on Enter, holds focus, and does not untoggle itself; copy takes the real URL to the clipboard, answers 'Copied' on the face of the control, says 'Link copied.' out loud, and reverts. Beyond that: every focusable element in every state in both rooms paints a measurable focus ring (walked with real Tab presses and verified by screenshot diff, not by outline-width); every control a thumb presses clears 44px on a coarse pointer across all fourteen states, both rooms, at 390 and 768; nothing is revealed only on hover and nothing reflows under the cursor; zero pageerrors and zero console errors across the whole sweep.
